lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Eight schools. Seven states. The Ivy League has trained presidents, justices, and a long line of governors. Tonight we are not going after the famous ones.
lines.caption: Eight schools. Seven states. The Ivy League has trained presidents, justices, and a long line of governors. Tonight we are not going after the famous ones.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Here is the game. Take the seven states that hold an Ivy League school. Count the governors from independence. Stop at number seven. Seven governors, seven minutes each, seven facts each. Lucky seven.
lines.caption: Here is the game. Take the seven states that hold an Ivy League school. Count the governors from independence. Stop at number seven. Seven governors, seven minutes each, seven facts each. Lucky seven.
lines.visual: card:Lucky Seven|The seventh governors of the Ivy states

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: And every episode asks the same three questions. Who got a say. Who got left out. And who paid for it.
lines.caption: And every episode asks the same three questions. Who got a say. Who got left out. And who paid for it.
lines.visual: card:Who got a say?|Who got left out? Who paid for it?

lines.speaker: G
lines.say: Matthew, I'm a Bowling Green guy. I know one governor from back east, and he was on the money.
lines.caption: Matthew, I'm a Bowling Green guy. I know one governor from back east, and he was on the money.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Then you are going to learn six new ones, Gary. We start in Connecticut.
lines.caption: Then you are going to learn six new ones, Gary. We start in Connecticut.

lines.speaker: CHAP
lines.visual: card:Chapter One · Connecticut|Roger Griswold · Yale, class of 1780

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Philadelphia. The winter of 1798. The United States Congress meets in Congress Hall, next to the State House. It is a young country, and the men in this room still treat it like a gentlemen's club.
lines.caption: Philadelphia. The winter of 1798. The United States Congress meets in Congress Hall, next to the State House. It is a young country, and the men in this room still treat it like a gentlemen's club.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: On January 30th, in a session on the House floor, Congressman Matthew Lyon of Vermont and Congressman Roger Griswold of Connecticut trade insults. Griswold asks him, mockingly, whether he'll be using his wooden sword, a jab at a disputed story that Lyon was drummed out of a command in the Revolution. Lyon spits tobacco juice in his face.
lines.caption: On January 30th, in a session on the House floor, Congressman Matthew Lyon of Vermont and Congressman Roger Griswold of Connecticut trade insults. Griswold asks him, mockingly, whether he'll be using his wooden sword, a jab at a disputed story that Lyon was drummed out of a command in the Revolution. Lyon spits tobacco juice in his face.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Two weeks later, February 15th, Griswold walks onto the floor with a hickory walking stick and goes after Lyon with it. Lyon grabs a pair of fireplace tongs from the hearth and fights back, right there, in the House of Representatives.
lines.caption: Two weeks later, February 15th, Griswold walks onto the floor with a hickory walking stick and goes after Lyon with it. Lyon grabs a pair of fireplace tongs from the hearth and fights back, right there, in the House of Representatives.

lines.speaker: G
lines.say: Now hold on. Fireplace tongs? In Congress?
lines.caption: Now hold on. Fireplace tongs? In Congress?

lines.speaker: YA
lines.say: Old boy, it was February. There was a fire. One makes do.
lines.caption: Old boy, it was February. There was a fire. One makes do.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: That is the man who would become Connecticut's seventh governor. And who he hit matters. Because Matthew Lyon was not a gentleman. Matthew Lyon had arrived in this country as a teenager who owed for his own passage.
lines.caption: That is the man who would become Connecticut's seventh governor. And who he hit matters. Because Matthew Lyon was not a gentleman. Matthew Lyon had arrived in this country as a teenager who owed for his own passage.
lines.visual: card:Fact 1 of 7|In 1798 Roger Griswold attacked a congressman with a cane on the House floor

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Roger Griswold was born May 21st, 1762, in Lyme, Connecticut, at the mouth of the Connecticut River. He was born into the governing class, and not by accident.
lines.caption: Roger Griswold was born May 21st, 1762, in Lyme, Connecticut, at the mouth of the Connecticut River. He was born into the governing class, and not by accident.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: His father, Matthew Griswold, became governor of Connecticut. His mother's father, Roger Wolcott, had been the colonial governor. Three generations, one family, one office.
lines.caption: His father, Matthew Griswold, became governor of Connecticut. His mother's father, Roger Wolcott, had been the colonial governor. Three generations, one family, one office.
lines.visual: card:Fact 2 of 7|His father and his grandfather were both governors of Connecticut

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: He entered Yale at fourteen and graduated in 1780, during the Revolution. Then he read law, and the law led where it always led for a family like his. Into politics.
lines.caption: He entered Yale at fourteen and graduated in 1780, during the Revolution. Then he read law, and the law led where it always led for a family like his. Into politics.

lines.speaker: YA
lines.say: Fourteen is young for Yale, I grant you. But the Griswolds were always early. To everything.
lines.caption: Fourteen is young for Yale, I grant you. But the Griswolds were always early. To everything.

lines.speaker: G
lines.say: Must be nice to have a reserved seat.
lines.caption: Must be nice to have a reserved seat.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Griswold went to Congress in 1795, a Federalist, the party of merchants, bankers and old New England families. He was sharp, he was proud, and he did not like the new men from the frontier.
lines.caption: Griswold went to Congress in 1795, a Federalist, the party of merchants, bankers and old New England families. He was sharp, he was proud, and he did not like the new men from the frontier.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Matthew Lyon was the new man from the frontier. Born in Ireland in 1749. He came to Connecticut in 1764, around fifteen years old, as a redemptioner. That means he couldn't pay for the ship, so his labor was sold to cover it. He worked off that debt for years before he bought his freedom in 1768.
lines.caption: Matthew Lyon was the new man from the frontier. Born in Ireland in 1749. He came to Connecticut in 1764, around fifteen years old, as a redemptioner. That means he couldn't pay for the ship, so his labor was sold to cover it. He worked off that debt for years before he bought his freedom in 1768.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Lyon went north to Vermont, served with the Green Mountain Boys in the Revolution, built a gristmill, a sawmill and a paper mill, started a newspaper, and got himself elected to Congress. A bound laborer who became a congressman. To a Yale man, that was the insult.
lines.caption: Lyon went north to Vermont, served with the Green Mountain Boys in the Revolution, built a gristmill, a sawmill and a paper mill, started a newspaper, and got himself elected to Congress. A bound laborer who became a congressman. To a Yale man, that was the insult.
lines.visual: card:Fact 3 of 7|Matthew Lyon came to America owing for his passage and worked it off as a bound laborer

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: After the brawl, a House committee recommended that both men be censured. The full House voted it down. Both men promised to keep the peace. Lyon apologized in writing.
lines.caption: After the brawl, a House committee recommended that both men be censured. The full House voted it down. Both men promised to keep the peace. Lyon apologized in writing.

lines.speaker: G
lines.say: So nobody got punished.
lines.caption: So nobody got punished.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Not that day, Gary. Wait for it.
lines.caption: Not that day, Gary. Wait for it.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Now, the counting. Connecticut's official list of governors goes all the way back to the colony's first governor, in 1639. On that list, Roger Griswold is number twenty-two.
lines.caption: Now, the counting. Connecticut's official list of governors goes all the way back to the colony's first governor, in 1639. On that list, Roger Griswold is number twenty-two.
lines.visual: card:Connecticut's official count|Starts in 1639 · Griswold is No. 22

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: But our game starts at independence. Jonathan Trumbull was governor when the colony became a state. Count from Trumbull, and you get Matthew Griswold, Samuel Huntington, Oliver Wolcott, Jonathan Trumbull Junior, John Treadwell, and then, number seven, Roger Griswold.
lines.caption: But our game starts at independence. Jonathan Trumbull was governor when the colony became a state. Count from Trumbull, and you get Matthew Griswold, Samuel Huntington, Oliver Wolcott, Jonathan Trumbull Junior, John Treadwell, and then, number seven, Roger Griswold.
lines.visual: card:Fact 4 of 7|Counted from independence, Roger Griswold is Connecticut's seventh governor

lines.speaker: YA
lines.say: Twenty-second or seventh. Either way, a Griswold. The club does keep its records.
lines.caption: Twenty-second or seventh. Either way, a Griswold. The club does keep its records.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Who gets counted is always a choice somebody made. Keep that in your pocket. It comes back all night.
lines.caption: Who gets counted is always a choice somebody made. Keep that in your pocket. It comes back all night.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Griswold was elected lieutenant governor in 1809 and governor in 1811. He was re-elected in the spring of 1812. And in June of 1812 the United States went to war with Britain.
lines.caption: Griswold was elected lieutenant governor in 1809 and governor in 1811. He was re-elected in the spring of 1812. And in June of 1812 the United States went to war with Britain.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: New England's merchants hated that war. It strangled their trade. So when Washington asked Connecticut for militia, Governor Griswold said no. He refused to put the state's militia under federal command.
lines.caption: New England's merchants hated that war. It strangled their trade. So when Washington asked Connecticut for militia, Governor Griswold said no. He refused to put the state's militia under federal command.
lines.visual: card:Fact 5 of 7|As governor in 1812 he refused to put Connecticut's militia under federal control

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Remember, this is a man who, back in 1801, turned down John Adams when Adams offered to make him Secretary of War. He did not want to run the federal army. He wanted to keep his own.
lines.caption: Remember, this is a man who, back in 1801, turned down John Adams when Adams offered to make him Secretary of War. He did not want to run the federal army. He wanted to keep his own.

lines.speaker: G
lines.say: Hold on. He says no to being in charge of the war, then he says no to the war?
lines.caption: Hold on. He says no to being in charge of the war, then he says no to the war?

lines.speaker: YA
lines.say: Consistency, Gary. He simply preferred his militia at home. Near the silver.
lines.caption: Consistency, Gary. He simply preferred his militia at home. Near the silver.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: So who was Matthew Lyon, really, by 1798? A mill owner. A printer whose paper was called The Farmers' Library. And when another paper wouldn't run his writing, he started one called The Scourge of Aristocracy. The Federalists nicknamed him the Spitting Lyon. To his voters, he was one of them.
lines.caption: So who was Matthew Lyon, really, by 1798? A mill owner. A printer whose paper was called The Farmers' Library. And when another paper wouldn't run his writing, he started one called The Scourge of Aristocracy. The Federalists nicknamed him the Spitting Lyon. To his voters, he was one of them.

lines.speaker: G
lines.say: The Scourge of Aristocracy? Okay, now I get why they wanted him gone.
lines.caption: The Scourge of Aristocracy? Okay, now I get why they wanted him gone.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Now back to the man with the tongs. That summer of 1798, Congress passed the Sedition Act. It made it a crime to publish false, scandalous or malicious writing against the government.
lines.caption: Now back to the man with the tongs. That summer of 1798, Congress passed the Sedition Act. It made it a crime to publish false, scandalous or malicious writing against the government.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: That October, Matthew Lyon became the first person put on trial under it, for what he had written about President Adams. He was convicted on October 10th, fined a thousand dollars, and locked in a cell in Vergennes, Vermont, for four months.
lines.caption: That October, Matthew Lyon became the first person put on trial under it, for what he had written about President Adams. He was convicted on October 10th, fined a thousand dollars, and locked in a cell in Vergennes, Vermont, for four months.
lines.visual: card:Fact 6 of 7|Lyon was the first person tried under the Sedition Act · four months in jail, a $1,000 fine

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: And from that cell, the voters of Vermont re-elected him to Congress, four thousand five hundred seventy-six votes to two thousand four hundred forty-four.
lines.caption: And from that cell, the voters of Vermont re-elected him to Congress, four thousand five hundred seventy-six votes to two thousand four hundred forty-four.

lines.speaker: G
lines.say: Okay. That's a heck of a comeback.
lines.caption: Okay. That's a heck of a comeback.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Same floor, same fight. The gentleman with the cane went home to Connecticut and kept rising. The servant with the tongs went to jail for what he wrote. One law for the club, another for the man who crashed it.
lines.caption: Same floor, same fight. The gentleman with the cane went home to Connecticut and kept rising. The servant with the tongs went to jail for what he wrote. One law for the club, another for the man who crashed it.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Roger Griswold did not get long in the governor's chair. He died in office on October 25th, 1812, in Norwich. He was fifty years old.
lines.caption: Roger Griswold did not get long in the governor's chair. He died in office on October 25th, 1812, in Norwich. He was fifty years old.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Before he ever sat in the governor's chair, Griswold sat on Connecticut's highest court, from 1807 to 1809. He was a presidential elector for the Federalist ticket of Charles Cotesworth Pinckney and Rufus King. Bench, ballot, and a seat at every table that mattered.
lines.caption: Before he ever sat in the governor's chair, Griswold sat on Connecticut's highest court, from 1807 to 1809. He was a presidential elector for the Federalist ticket of Charles Cotesworth Pinckney and Rufus King. Bench, ballot, and a seat at every table that mattered.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: And there's one more thing on his record. In 1803, when Thomas Jefferson bought Louisiana, Griswold was one of the New England Federalists who talked about taking New England out of the Union. Their region was losing power to the South and the West, and they did not like it.
lines.caption: And there's one more thing on his record. In 1803, when Thomas Jefferson bought Louisiana, Griswold was one of the New England Federalists who talked about taking New England out of the Union. Their region was losing power to the South and the West, and they did not like it.
lines.visual: card:1803|New England Federalists talk about leaving the Union

lines.speaker: G
lines.say: Wait. The governor who wouldn't send his militia to the war also wanted to leave the country?
lines.caption: Wait. The governor who wouldn't send his militia to the war also wanted to leave the country?

lines.speaker: YA
lines.say: Gary, a gentleman never leaves. He simply considers other clubs.
lines.caption: Gary, a gentleman never leaves. He simply considers other clubs.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Remember that one, because two of our seven governors were in that same secession conversation in 1803. You'll meet the other one in New Hampshire. He lived long enough to call it a mistake.
lines.caption: Remember that one, because two of our seven governors were in that same secession conversation in 1803. You'll meet the other one in New Hampshire. He lived long enough to call it a mistake.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: At home, Griswold married Fanny Rogers, and they had ten children. His grandson, another Matthew Griswold, went to Congress from Pennsylvania in the 1890s. In this family, public office was the family business.
lines.caption: At home, Griswold married Fanny Rogers, and they had ten children. His grandson, another Matthew Griswold, went to Congress from Pennsylvania in the 1890s. In this family, public office was the family business.

lines.speaker: YA
lines.say: Ten children. Good heavens. Think of the tuition.
lines.caption: Ten children. Good heavens. Think of the tuition.

lines.speaker: G
lines.say: Think of the canes.
lines.caption: Think of the canes.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Three years later, Connecticut named a town for him. Griswold, Connecticut, incorporated in 1815, out in the eastern hills.
lines.caption: Three years later, Connecticut named a town for him. Griswold, Connecticut, incorporated in 1815, out in the eastern hills.
lines.visual: card:Fact 7 of 7|The town of Griswold, Connecticut, incorporated in 1815, is named for him

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Yale gave him an honorary law degree in 1812, the year he died. His grave is in the family cemetery at Black Hall, in Old Lyme.
lines.caption: Yale gave him an honorary law degree in 1812, the year he died. His grave is in the family cemetery at Black Hall, in Old Lyme.

lines.speaker: YA
lines.say: A Yale man, a Yale father, a governor's grandson. Boola boola, I suppose.
lines.caption: A Yale man, a Yale father, a governor's grandson. Boola boola, I suppose.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: A town for the man with the cane. A jail cell for the man with the tongs. Connecticut's lucky number seven.
lines.caption: A town for the man with the cane. A jail cell for the man with the tongs. Connecticut's lucky number seven.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Connecticut. Keep it real.
lines.caption: Connecticut. Keep it real.
